cards.title: Peter W. Allsopp
cards.sub: 1996 · Bank of England, chairing the BIS/CPSS steering group
cards.prompt: Who chaired the G10 steering group behind the 1996 settlement-risk report, and what was that group actually trying to do? It did not build a settlement system.
cards.answer: Peter W. Allsopp, of the Bank of England. The group's job was to define the exposure precisely enough to be measured and to push banks to control their own — it named the property (payment versus payment) rather than building the thing that delivers it.
cards.body: Allsopp chaired the CPSS Steering Group on Settlement Risk in Foreign Exchange Transactions, and was retiring from the Bank of England the year it reported. The group shipped no infrastructure. It defined the exposure well enough to measure, and wrote down the property the market was missing.

cards.title: Bankhaus Herstatt
cards.prompt: A Cologne bank was shut down one Wednesday afternoon in 1974. Why did the hour of the closure, rather than the size of the bank, cost its counterparties the full principal?
cards.answer: The licence went at 15:30 CET — after Germany's interbank payment system had closed for the day, while New York was still open. Counterparties had already paid Deutsche marks irrevocably that morning; Herstatt's New York correspondent then stopped the matching dollar payments. The first leg had committed and the second never ran.
cards.body: German authorities closed Bankhaus Herstatt at 15:30 CET on 26 June 1974. Counterparties had irrevocably paid Deutsche marks in Frankfurt; the dollars never left New York. BIS estimated the transactions awaiting settlement at $200 million. New York banks then froze their own payments, and gross funds through the city's netting system fell an estimated 60% in three days.

cards.title: Settlement Risk in Foreign Exchange Transactions
cards.sub: March 1996 · CPSS report, Basle (the Allsopp Report)
cards.prompt: Which document can you open today for the one-sentence definition of atomic settlement across two payment systems, and what venue and month are printed on it?
cards.answer: 'Settlement Risk in Foreign Exchange Transactions', prepared by the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems of the G10 central banks — Basle, March 1996, later indexed as CPMI Papers no 17. The definition is in its glossary, under payment versus payment.
cards.body: The glossary entry is the whole idea in one line: "Payment versus payment (PVP): a mechanism in a foreign exchange settlement system that ensures that a final transfer of one currency occurs if and only if a final transfer of the other currency or currencies takes place."

cards.title: The Basel Committee
cards.sub: end of 1974 · G10 central bank Governors
cards.prompt: Herstatt's failure produced a permanent institution within months. Name it, say who created it and when, and say when it first met.
cards.answer: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision — initially the Committee on Banking Regulations and Supervisory Practices — established by the central bank Governors of the G10 at the end of 1974. Its first meeting was in February 1975.
cards.body: The G10 Governors set it up at the end of 1974, in the aftermath of "serious disturbances in international currency and banking markets (notably the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt in West Germany)". First meeting: February 1975. Every Basel capital accord descends from that afternoon in Cologne.

cards.title: CLS Bank, and what it still cannot reach
cards.prompt: The industry did eventually build the coordinator. Name it, give its launch year, and give the two limits that stop it covering all foreign exchange settlement.
cards.answer: CLS Bank, live September 2002. It settles only inside one daily window — 07:00 to 12:00 CET, against strict hourly pay-in deadlines — and only in a fixed currency list, 18 as of 2022. So $2.2 trillion a day was still settling at risk in April 2022.
cards.body: CLS went live in September 2002 with seven currencies, settling payment-versus-payment inside a 07:00-12:00 CET window against strict hourly pay-in deadlines. By 2022 it covered 18. BIS still measured $2.2 trillion of daily FX turnover settling without that protection in April 2022.
